summary:
Arqueonautas is an interactive website that turns the equipment NASA left on the Moon and Mars into a “space archaeology” museum for kids and teens. Visitors choose a world and explore beacons on the planet. Each beacon tells the story of a mission, from Surveyor 3 and the Apollo lunar rovers to Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity, with photos, voice narration, and kid and expert versions of every story.

To turn learning into a game, each story earns a stamp in an explorer passport that leads to badges and a printable certificate. A robot guide helps on the first visit. The lab offers experiments and mini-games that show real science: landing under different gravity, driving a rover with a signal delay, cleaning InSight’s solar panels, and comparing how a hammer and a feather fall.

The project matters because it shows that these objects aren’t trash: they are traces of our history of exploration. In this way it sparks scientific curiosity and brings space science to new generations in an accessible, fun way.
details:
What it does and how it works
Arqueonautas is an interactive website about the hardware NASA left on the Moon and Mars. The home screen shows a single planet split diagonally: half Moon, half Mars. Shooting stars cross the sky and animated landers touch down from time to time. Mars landers use a parachute and then rockets, while Moon landers use rockets only. Clicking “Explore” zooms into a world, where glowing beacons mark 19 missions, from Surveyor 3 and the Apollo lunar rovers to Viking, Sojourner, Spirit & Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity, plus deep-space probes shown on a separate orbit. Each beacon opens a card with photos, the mission story, a fun fact, and a “Listen” button with cinematic narration. A timeline slider from 1964 to 2024 reveals the missions in the order they arrived.

Benefits

  • Learning as a game: every story earns a stamp in an explorer passport, and stamps unlock badges and a printable certificate.
  • For different ages and reading levels: a Kids/Expert switch and voice narration adapt the content.
  • Hands-on science: the Lab & Games section turns abstract concepts into experiences. Kids land a spacecraft under Moon or Mars gravity, drive a rover with a radio delay, clean dust off InSight’s solar panels, compare their weight on each world, send a message at the speed of light, and watch a hammer and a feather fall together, as in the Apollo 15 experiment.
  • Easy to use anywhere: it works in any browser, on computers and phones, with nothing to install.

Expected impact
We want children and teens to see these objects not as space junk but as an archaeological record of human exploration. The project aims to spark curiosity about planetary science and engineering, give teachers a free classroom resource, and help students understand why missions are designed the way they are.

Tools and technologies

  • Code: HTML5, CSS3 and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks.
  • Browser features: Canvas API for the mini-games, SVG for illustrations, Web Audio API for sound effects, Web Speech API as a backup narrator, and localStorage to save progress.
  • Audio: narration voices generated with ElevenLabs. Background music composed by code in Python with NumPy, and reverb added with FFmpeg.
  • Images: NASA public-domain photos. AI-generated artwork is clearly labeled “Illustration” on the page.
  • Fonts and hosting: Google Fonts and Netlify.
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) helped with coding, design and testing.

Creativity
The project frames space exploration as archaeology, with “beacons,” “files” and a passport, and the stories are told from the point of view of what was left behind. The interactions are built around the stories themselves: each “Try it!” button links a mission to a game that teaches what made it special. The planet and the deep-space orbit organize the content visually, and an original robot guide, ARQ-1, welcomes first-time visitors.

Factors our team considered

  • Ages and reading levels: Kids/Expert modes, narration, large buttons and a step-by-step guide.
  • Accuracy: content based on NASA sources, with a clear distinction between real photos and illustrations.
  • Difficulty: games tuned so they challenge kids without frustrating them. For example, Mars landing uses a parachute and extra fuel.
  • Accessibility: keyboard controls, respect for the “reduced motion” setting, and a sound on/off option.
  • Devices: a responsive layout for desktop, laptop and mobile, with touch controls.
  • Cost and reach: free hosting, no installation, and original or public-domain media to avoid copyright issues.
